claims.text: Conventional static EAM potentials in TOR-TILD poorly represent the configurational diversity of the ab initio liquid state.
Replacing EAM references with an iteratively refined machine-learning potential will more accurately represent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The proposed machine-learning potential is trained on ab initio configurations sampled in the high-temperature, near-melting regime.
The proposed method applies to both solid and liquid high-entropy-alloy states.
The applicable alloys are nearly equiatomic systems with approximately five to seven principal elements.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9–1.1 times the melting temperature.
Training on diverse high-temperature ab initio configurations enables the machine-learning potential to capture the wide variety of local atomic environments in the liquid.
The machine-learning potential can capture many-body interactions relevant to the liquid alloy.
Iterative retraining on ab initio snapshots produces a more faithful representation of the ab initio energy landscape.
A more faithful representation of the ab initio energy landscape improves phase-space overlap between the reference and target systems.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration discrepancies.
The proposed method will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 25–50% relative to static EAM-based TOR-TILD calculations.
The proposed method will accelerate free-energy convergence.
The proposed method will produce more reliable free-energy estimates.
Performance may be limited for alloys with extreme compositional variation.
Performance may be limited under conditions far from the melting regime.
The magnitude of the improvement depends on the quality of the ab initio training dataset and the particular alloy composition.

Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement of at least 25% in path mismatch, or failure to improve phase-space overlap and free-energy convergence relative to static EAM, would falsify the hypothesis.
